01.r: Ties Judas's act to the moment of the condemnation.
01.n: Abbott-Smith: 'then, at that time', of events at the same time or following on.

02.r: Judas sees how things have turned out.
02.n: An aorist participle: the seeing comes before the regret and the return of the money.

03.r: The disciple who handed Jesus over.
03.n: Abbott-Smith notes the name is the Hebrew יְהוּדָה, Judah, and lists the patriarch Judah as its first bearer.

04.r: The article turns the participle into a description of Judas.

05.r: Describes Judas by what he did: he handed Jesus over.
05.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to give or hand over to another'. A present participle, used almost as a title, 'the one handing him over'; the translations' 'betrayed' gives the act its moral name.

08.r: The one Judas handed over had been judged guilty.
08.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to give judgment against, condemn'. The Greek says only 'he'; the BSB names Jesus.

09.r: Judas is sorry for what he has done.
09.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to regret, repent' and names μετανοέω, to change one's mind, repent, as a related word, adding that the distinction between the two is difficult to maintain by usage. The older translations' 'repented himself' renders this word, not μετανοέω; the BSB has 'filled with remorse'.

10.r: He took the silver back to those who paid it.
10.n: Abbott-Smith: the plain verb 'to turn', and he notes that in this verse it equals the compound ἀποστρέφω, 'to bring back'.

11.r: The silver already agreed and paid.

12.r: The full sum, all of it returned.

13.r: The coins he had been paid.
13.n: Abbott-Smith gives the proper sense as 'a piece of silver', and the New Testament senses 'silver' and 'money'. The plural counts pieces. The YLT's 'silverlings' is an old word for silver coins.

14.r: The article; 'to' comes from the dative case of the nouns that follow.

15.r: The leading priests, those who had paid him.
15.n: This study renders the word 'high priest' in the singular. In the plural, as here, Abbott-Smith gives 'chief priests, including ex-high-priests and members of high-priestly families', so 'chief priests' is used.

16.r: Joins the elders to the chief priests.

18.r: The senior men of the people who sat with the chief priests.
18.n: A comparative of the word for 'old man', so literally 'older men'; Abbott-Smith gives first 'of age, elder'. English 'presbyter', and through it 'priest', come from this word.

tr_note: Where our text has ἔστρεψεν, 'turned, brought back', the Textus Receptus has the compound ἀπέστρεψεν, 'returned'; it also repeats the article before 'elders', 'to the elders'. The KJV's 'brought again' gives the same sense either way, and the repeated article shows only in the YLT's 'and to the elders'.
